title: DNS Deep Dive
intro: 'It's always DNS' is a joke because it's so often true. Knowing exactly which resolver answered, and from where, turns DNS from a mystery into a two-minute check.

steps.prompt: See which DNS servers this machine is configured to use.
steps.explanation: Lookups go to 10.0.0.2 (typically the cloud VPC's resolver). The 'search' line means a short name like 'db' is also tried as 'db.internal.example.com'.
steps.why: The search domain explains a lot of 'why does this short name resolve here but not on my laptop' confusion. In Kubernetes pods, this file is exactly how short service names like 'db' get resolved.

steps.prompt: Check whether /etc/hosts overrides anything — it's consulted BEFORE DNS.
steps.explanation: A hardcoded entry pins api.internal.example.com to 10.0.4.99, regardless of what DNS says.
steps.why: Forgotten /etc/hosts entries are a classic source of 'DNS looks right but this one server keeps going to the old IP' (see networking-incident-003). dig bypasses /etc/hosts; your application does not.

steps.prompt: Query a specific public resolver (8.8.8.8) directly, bypassing your local configuration.
steps.fake_output:
;; ANSWER SECTION:
api.example.com.   300   IN   A   198.51.100.20
;; SERVER: 8.8.8.8#53(8.8.8.8)
steps.explanation: The 300 is the TTL — resolvers may cache this answer for up to 5 minutes.
steps.why: Comparing your local resolver's answer against a public one isolates whether a problem is your resolver (stale cache, split-horizon config) or the actual DNS records.

steps.prompt: Look up the mail servers (MX records) for example.com.
steps.fake_output:
;; ANSWER SECTION:
example.com.  3600  IN  MX  10 mx1.mailprovider.com.
example.com.  3600  IN  MX  20 mx2.mailprovider.com.
steps.explanation: Lower preference number (10) is tried first.
steps.why: dig queries A records by default. Specifying the record type (MX, TXT, CNAME, NS) is how you debug email delivery, domain-verification TXT records, and CNAME chains.

steps.prompt: Reverse-lookup which hostname an unknown IP in your logs belongs to.
steps.explanation: A PTR record maps an IP back to a name.
steps.why: Useful for identifying traffic sources in logs. Not every IP has a PTR record, and PTR records can say anything — treat them as a hint, not proof of identity.

steps.prompt: Trace the full resolution path from the root servers down, to see where a lookup actually gets its answer.
steps.fake_output:
.            518400 IN NS a.root-servers.net.
com.         172800 IN NS a.gtld-servers.net.
example.com. 172800 IN NS ns1.dnsprovider.com.
api.example.com. 300 IN A  198.51.100.20
steps.explanation: Root → .com → the domain's authoritative nameservers → the final record, with no caching involved.
steps.why: +trace asks the authoritative servers directly, so it shows the TRUE current record. When a DNS change 'isn't working', this tells you whether the change is live at the source and you're just waiting on caches (TTL) to expire.
